note: Attacker-controlled fvar table header is read from the font stream into fvar_head, including axisCount and instanceCount fields.

code: if ( fvar_head.axisCount > GX_MAX_AXES ) return FT_THROW( Invalid_Table );
note: axisCount is validated only against the upper bound GX_MAX_AXES; a value of 0 passes this check because there is no axisCount == 0 rejection in this vulnerable revision.

code: if ( fvar_head.instanceCount > GX_MAX_INSTANCES ) return FT_THROW( Invalid_Table );
note: instanceCount is validated only against the upper bound; a small value such as 1 passes.

code: mmvar_len = sizeof ( FT_MM_Var ) + fvar_head.axisCount * sizeof ( FT_Var_Axis ) + fvar_head.instanceCount * sizeof ( FT_Var_Named_Style );
note: mmvar_len is computed from the attacker-controlled axisCount (0) and instanceCount, so the allocated FT_MM_Var block contains no FT_Var_Axis entries.
A heap buffer of mmvar_len bytes is allocated; with axisCount == 0 the axis array region has zero length.
The axis pointer is set to the first byte after the FT_MM_Var header, which is also the end of the allocation when axisCount == 0.
With axisCount == 0 the loop that initializes axes is skipped, so no out-of-bounds write occurs here; the vulnerable read is reached later when the caller iterates over mmvar->axis.
num_axis is set to the attacker-controlled value 0, so downstream code that trusts num_axis will not iterate; the overflow instead occurs in the caller that assumes at least one axis exists.
num_namedstyles is set from instanceCount; the named-style array is laid out immediately after the (empty) axis array.
namedstyle points to mmvar->axis + 0, i.e. the same address as the end of the FT_MM_Var header; the named-style records are then read from the stream into this region.

code: for ( j = 0; j < fvar_head.axisCount; j++ ) mmvar->namedstyle[i].coords[j] = ...;
note: The named-style coordinate loop iterates axisCount (0) times, so no write occurs; the malformed zero-axis fvar is accepted and returned to the caller.
TT_Get_MM_Var returns success with a zero-axis FT_MM_Var object, leaving the font flagged as a Multiple-Master font.
The gvar table header is parsed; its axisCount field is attacker-controlled and is not cross-checked against the fvar axisCount.

code: if ( gvar_head.axisCount != face->blend->mmvar->num_axis ) return FT_THROW( Invalid_Table );
note: gvar axisCount is compared to the fvar num_axis (0); a gvar table with axisCount 0 passes this check.
blend->num_axis is set to 0, so later variation application loops are skipped and no overflow occurs in gvar processing itself.
The zero-axis case is handled in the location path, so the crash must occur in the fvar parsing path itself when the caller dereferences the zero-length axis array.

In the vulnerable revision the axis initialization loop is guarded only by axisCount, so with axisCount == 0 this line is not executed; the heap-buffer-overflow READ 8 is instead triggered by the fuzzer harness reading mmvar->axis[0] after TT_Get_MM_Var returns, because the axis array has zero length but the caller assumes at least one axis exists.

The zero-axis FT_MM_Var object is returned; the ftfuzzer target then reads mmvar->axis[0].name / .def / .minimum / .maximum (8-byte reads) past the end of the heap allocation, producing the heap-buffer-overflow READ 8.
